The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $a\le b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). The function $f$ is
**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F,G\in AC[a,b]$,
$$\int_a^bFG'+\int_a^bF'G=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a).$$

Throughout, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$ is written
$\lambda_n$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]), and
$\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb R$ is the copy of the integers
([[def-integers]]).

**The torus.** Let $q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the
canonical projection of the quotient of the additive group $\mathbb R$ by its
subgroup $\mathbb Z$, carrying the quotient topology
([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-topological-space]]); we write
$[t]:=q(t)=t+\mathbb Z$. Thus $[s]=[t]$ exactly when $s-t\in\mathbb Z$. The map
$q$ is continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and $\mathbb T$ is a compact
Hausdorff space homeomorphic to the Euclidean unit circle.

**Fundamental domain.** Every class has exactly one representative in $[0,1)$:
for $t\in\mathbb R$ the integer part $n=\lfloor t\rfloor$ satisfies
$n\le t<n+1$, so $t-n\in[0,1)$ represents $[t]$ ([[lem-integer-part]]); and if
$s,t\in[0,1)$ satisfy $s-t\in\mathbb Z$, then $|s-t|<1$ forces $s=t$.
Consequently the map $[0,1)\to\mathbb T$, $t\mapsto[t]$, is a bijection.

**Topological checks.** The closed interval $[0,1]$ is compact by [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and maps onto $\mathbb T$, so the quotient is compact by [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. The map $t\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is continuous by [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], and is constant on quotient fibres by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]. It induces a continuous map $\varphi:\mathbb T\to S^1$ by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The bijection of $[0,2\pi)$ with the circle in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]], together with the unique representatives in $[0,1)$, makes $\varphi$ bijective. The Euclidean circle is Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]], so the compact-to-Hausdorff clause of [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]] makes $\varphi$ a homeomorphism. In particular $\mathbb T$ is Hausdorff.

The map $q$ is open: for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, its saturation $q^{-1}[q[U]]=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}(U+k)$ is open. The images under $q$ of rational-endpoint open intervals form a countable base: if $q(t)\in V$ with $V$ open, choose such an interval containing $t$ and contained in $q^{-1}[V]$. Its image is an open neighbourhood contained in $V$.

**The measure.** For a Borel set $E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) the preimage $q^{-1}[E]$ is a Borel subset of
$\mathbb R$, because $q$ is continuous
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]), hence Lebesgue
measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). Define

$$m_{\mathbb T}(E):=\lambda_1\bigl(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)\bigr) ,$$

the value at $q^{-1}[E]$ of the same-ambient restriction of $\lambda_1$ to $[0,1)$
([[def-restriction-of-a-measure]]).

This is a measure on $\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$ by [[prop-restriction-is-a-measure]]:
the assignment $E\mapsto\lambda_1(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1))$ is the composition of the
restriction measure with the inverse image along $q$, and inverse images preserve
the empty set, complements and countable unions, while countable additivity is
that of $\lambda_1$. It is a **probability measure**:
$m_{\mathbb T}(\mathbb T)=\lambda_1([0,1))=1$
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]). Thus
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T})$ is a probability measure space
([[def-measure-space]], [[def-measure]]).

**The integral.** For a Borel measurable $F:\mathbb T\to[0,+\infty]$, define

$$\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}:=\int_{[0,1)}F\circ q\,d\lambda_1 .$$

The defining integral is meaningful because $F\circ q$ is Borel
([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]],
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]). The assignment agrees with
$E\mapsto m_{\mathbb T}(E)$ on indicators, and it is additive and homogeneous on
finite nonnegative simple functions; for a sequence $0\le F_0\le F_1\le\cdots$
with $F_n\uparrow F$ pointwise the identity passes to the limit because
$F_n\circ q\uparrow F\circ q$ and monotone convergence holds for $\lambda_1$
([[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]],
[[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]). For real or complex integrable
$F$ the integral is defined by decomposition into nonnegative parts or into real
and imaginary parts, and it is linear
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]],
[[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]). In particular
$\int_{\mathbb T}1\,dm_{\mathbb T}=1$, and the same formula holds with $[0,1)$
replaced by any half-open interval $[a,a+1)$ or $(a,a+1]$, by the periodicity of
$q^{-1}[E]$ and the translation invariance of $\lambda_1$
([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]).

**Translation invariance.** For $y\in\mathbb R$ the map
$\tau_y:\mathbb T\to\mathbb T$, $\tau_y([t]):=[t+y]$, is well defined (if
$s-t\in\mathbb Z$ then $(s+y)-(t+y)\in\mathbb Z$) and continuous, because it is
induced by the continuous map $t\mapsto q(t+y)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb T$. This composite is constant on the fibres of $q$, since $q(t)=q(s)$ implies $q(t+y)=q(s+y)$ ([[thm-quotient-universal-property]]). It preserves
$m_{\mathbb T}$: write $y=n+r$ with $n=\lfloor y\rfloor$ and $r\in[0,1)$, put
$A:=q^{-1}[E]$ and use that $A-n=A$ and that
$A\cap[0,1)=\bigl(A\cap[0,r)\bigr)\cup\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)$ while
$A\cap[r,r+1)=\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)\cup\bigl((A\cap[0,r))+1\bigr)$, so that

$$m_{\mathbb T}(\tau_y^{-1}E)=\lambda_1\bigl((A-y)\cap[0,1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[r,r+1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[0,1)\bigr)=m_{\mathbb T}(E),$$

the middle equality by translation invariance of $\lambda_1$. Hence
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T},\tau_y)$ is a measure-preserving
system for every $y$, and the published integral-invariance theorem gives
$\int_{\mathbb T}F\circ\tau_y\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}$
for every measurable $F\ge0$ and every integrable $F$
([[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]],
[[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]]). This is the
**normalized Haar integral** of $\mathbb T$; abstract Haar theory is not
invoked.

**The finite torus.** For a natural $n\ge1$ put
$\mathbb T^n:=\mathbb R^n/\mathbb Z^n$ with the quotient topology of the
canonical projection $q_n$, and define

$$m_{\mathbb T^n}(E):=\lambda_n\bigl(q_n^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)^n\bigr),\qquad \int_{\mathbb T^n}F\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}:=\int_{[0,1)^n}F\circ q_n\,d\lambda_n .$$

Coordinatewise integer parts give unique representatives in $[0,1)^n$, and the continuous quotient map sends the compact cube $[0,1]^n$ onto $\mathbb T^n$. Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection
$\Phi:\mathbb T^n\to(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n$ by the universal property. Its
domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite
product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection
theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the
finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]],
[[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]],
[[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters
$x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact
Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets
of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give
$m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so
$m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure
$m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$
([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures,
and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them
on the entire Borel sigma-algebra
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on
$\mathbb T^n$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: Let $m=\mathbb E[g(U)]$ and $h(x)=g(a+Lx)-m$ for $0\le x\le1$. Define $H(t)=h(2t)$ for $0\le t\le1/2$ and $H(t)=h(2-2t)$ for $1/2\le t\le1$, then extend $H$ periodically to $\mathbb T$. The two absolutely continuous pieces match at $t=1/2$, and $H(0)=H(1)$. A finite paste of absolutely continuous pieces with matching endpoint values is absolutely continuous: split every interval crossing the junction into its at most two pieces and apply [F1] on each piece with half the error tolerance. Thus $H$ is absolutely continuous on the period interval. Its mean is zero, $\|H\|_{L^2(\mathbb T)}^2=\operatorname{Var}(g(U))$, and affine changes of variables give $\|H'\|_{L^2(\mathbb T)}^2=4L^2\mathbb E|g'(U)|^2$.

For each integer $n$, apply integration by parts [F2] to $H(t)e^{-2\pi int}$ on $[0,1]$, taking real and imaginary parts. The boundary term vanishes since $H(0)=H(1)$ and $e^{-2\pi in}=1$, giving $\widehat{H'}(n)=2\pi in\widehat H(n)$. Parseval [F4] and the zero mean in step 1.1 yield $$\|H'\|_2^2=\sum_{n\ne0}4\pi^2n^2|\widehat H(n)|^2\ge4\pi^2\sum_{n\ne0}|\widehat H(n)|^2=4\pi^2\|H\|_2^2.$$ Substituting the two norm identities from step 1.1 and dividing by $4\pi^2$ proves the claimed bound. Equality holds for $g(x)=\cos(\pi(x-a)/L)$: its mean is zero, its variance is $1/2$, and its derivative second moment is $\pi^2/(2L^2)$. Hence the constant $L^2/\pi^2$ is sharp.

Let $d\ge1$ be finite, let $(E_j,\mathcal E_j,\mu_j)$ be probability spaces,
and let $(E,\mathcal E,\mu)=\prod_{j=1}^d(E_j,\mathcal E_j,\mu_j)$ be their
finite product with product sigma-algebra and product probability. Write
$[d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}$. For $J\subseteq[d]$, let $E_J$ and $\mu_J$ denote the
corresponding coordinate product; the empty product is a one-point probability
space. For real $f\in L^2(\mu)$, define the coordinate average
$$P_Jf(x_J)=\int_{E_{[d]\setminus J}}f(x_J,z_{[d]\setminus J})\,d\mu_{[d]\setminus J}(z_{[d]\setminus J})$$
for almost every $x_J$ for which the section is integrable, and assign zero on
the exceptional null set. Regard $P_Jf$ also as a function on the full product
that is constant in the coordinates outside $J$. The conventions are
$P_{[d]}f=f$ as an $L^2$ class and $P_\varnothing f=\int f\,d\mu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

If representatives $f$ and $\tilde f$ agree almost everywhere, Tonelli applied to $|f-\tilde f|^2$ shows their sections agree almost everywhere for almost every $x_J$; their averages therefore define the same almost-sure class. Fubini gives measurability of the section-average function.

On almost every section, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|P_Jf(x_J)|^2\le\int|f(x_J,z)|^2\,d\mu_{-J}(z)$ because $\mu_{-J}$ has mass one. Integrating in $x_J$ and using Tonelli yields $\|P_Jf\|_2^2\le\|f\|_2^2$, so $P_J$ is a contraction. Averaging a function already independent of $z_{-J}$ leaves it unchanged, hence $P_J^2=P_J$.

For $f,g\in L^2$, Cauchy–Schwarz makes $fg$ integrable. Fubini in the two groups of coordinates gives $\langle P_Jf,g\rangle=\int_{E_J}(P_Jf)(P_Jg)\,d\mu_J=\langle f,P_Jg\rangle$. Thus $P_J$ is self-adjoint.

Applying $P_K$ and then $P_J$ integrates over the coordinates outside $K$, then over the coordinates in $K\setminus J$. Repeated finite-product Fubini permits this order and identifies the iterated integral with integration over the complement of $J\cap K$. The equality holds almost everywhere by [F3], including when either set is empty or full, so $P_JP_Kf=P_{J\cap K}f$ in $L^2$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ embeds isometrically as a closed subspace of real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. For $X\in L^2(P)$, $U=E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is its orthogonal projection onto this subspace. It uniquely minimizes $E[(X-Z)^2]$ over $Z\in L^2(\mathcal G)$ as an almost-sure class.

Assume AC. On a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, let
$d\ge1$ be finite and let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$ be any jointly distributed
finite family of random elements. Let $Y=f(X)\in L^2(\mathbb P)$, and put
$V=\operatorname{Var}(Y)$. For $S\subseteq[d]$, set
$\mathcal G_S=\sigma(X_j:j\in S)$, with $\mathcal G_\varnothing=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$, and
$$v(S)=\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal G_S]).$$
If $V>0$, let $\mathfrak S_d$ be the set of all $d!$ permutations of $[d]$,
and let $P_i^\pi$ contain the indices occurring before $i$ in $\pi$. The
**Shapley effect** of coordinate $i$ under this convention is
$$\phi_i=\frac{1}{d!\,V}\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak S_d}\bigl(v(P_i^\pi\cup\{i\})-v(P_i^\pi)\bigr).$$
If $V=0$, the normalized effects are undefined. This definition is for
dependent inputs as well as independent ones; the independent Sobol ANOVA
components are not used to define $v$.

**Input:** A finite player set $[d]$, an exact oracle for $v(S)$ at every
$S\subseteq[d]$, and a known $V>0$ satisfying $v(\varnothing)=0$ and
$v([d])=V$. In the sensitivity application, $v$ is the conditional-projection
variance game of [[def-dependent-input-shapley-effects]].

1. Initialize $A_i=0$ for every $i\in[d]$.
2. For each of the $d!$ permutations $\pi$, traverse its entries in order. Start
   with $S=\varnothing$. At entry $i$, add $v(S\cup\{i\})-v(S)$ to $A_i$ and
   replace $S$ by $S\cup\{i\}$.
3. Return $\phi_i=A_i/(d!V)$ for all $i$.

The domain excludes $V=0$ and unavailable coalition values; the procedure does
not approximate conditional expectations or their numerical errors.

derivations.claim: Fix $S\subseteq T\subseteq[d]$, and write $m_S=\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal G_S]$ and $m_T=\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal G_T]$. The subspaces of $\mathcal G_S$- and $\mathcal G_T$-measurable $L^2$ functions are nested. For every $h$ in the smaller subspace, $\langle m_T-Y,h\rangle=0$ because $h$ also belongs to the larger subspace. Thus $m_T$ and $Y$ have the same orthogonal projection onto the smaller subspace, namely $m_S$, so $m_T-m_S\perp m_S-\mathbb EY$. Pythagoras gives $v(T)-v(S)=\|m_T-m_S\|_2^2\ge0$.

For any permutation $\pi$, sum the successive increments $v(P_i^\pi\cup\{i\})-v(P_i^\pi)$ in the order of that permutation. Every intermediate coalition value appears once positively and once negatively, leaving $v([d])-v(\varnothing)$. The projection in [F1] fixes $Y$, so $v([d])=V$; the empty-set projection is constant $\mathbb EY$, so $v(\varnothing)=0$. Step 1.1 gives monotonicity, so these endpoint values imply $0\le v(S)\le V$ for every coalition. Thus the increments sum to $V$.
Each increment in step 2.1 is nonnegative by step 1.1. Average over the finite set of $d!$ permutations and divide by $V>0$. The resulting effects are nonnegative and their sum is $V/V=1$.

In the procedure [F3], before each entry $i$ of a permutation $\pi$, the current set $S$ is exactly $P_i^\pi$: it starts empty and each preceding entry is added once. Thus the increment added to $A_i$ is $v(P_i^\pi\cup\{i\})-v(P_i^\pi)$. There are $d!$ permutations with $d$ entries each, so the loops perform finitely many iterations and at most $2d\,d!$ exact coalition-value calls; every queried value is available by the stated oracle input. Summing the increments gives $A_i=\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak S_d}(v(P_i^\pi\cup\{i\})-v(P_i^\pi))$, and division by $d!V$ returns exactly $\phi_i$ by [F2].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. On a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, let
$d\ge1$ be finite and let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$ be any jointly distributed
finite family of random elements. Let $Y=f(X)\in L^2(\mathbb P)$, and put
$V=\operatorname{Var}(Y)$. For $S\subseteq[d]$, set
$\mathcal G_S=\sigma(X_j:j\in S)$, with $\mathcal G_\varnothing=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$, and
$$v(S)=\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal G_S]).$$
If $V>0$, let $\mathfrak S_d$ be the set of all $d!$ permutations of $[d]$,
and let $P_i^\pi$ contain the indices occurring before $i$ in $\pi$. The
**Shapley effect** of coordinate $i$ under this convention is
$$\phi_i=\frac{1}{d!\,V}\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak S_d}\bigl(v(P_i^\pi\cup\{i\})-v(P_i^\pi)\bigr).$$
If $V=0$, the normalized effects are undefined. This definition is for
dependent inputs as well as independent ones; the independent Sobol ANOVA
components are not used to define $v$.

**Input:** A finite player set $[d]$, exact coalition values $v(S)$ with
$v(\varnothing)=0$, $v([d])=V>0$, and a declared integer sample size $n\ge2$.

1. Draw $n$ independent permutations $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n$, each uniformly
   from the $d!$ permutations of $[d]$.
2. For each row $r$ and each $i$, compute
   $\Delta_i^{(r)}=v(P_i^{\pi_r}\cup\{i\})-v(P_i^{\pi_r})$.
3. Return $\widehat\phi_i=(nV)^{-1}\sum_r\Delta_i^{(r)}$ and the standard-error
   covariance estimate $\widehat\Sigma_\Delta/(nV^2)$, where
   $\widehat\Sigma_\Delta=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_r(\Delta^{(r)}-\bar\Delta)
   (\Delta^{(r)}-\bar\Delta)^{\mathsf T}$.

The exact conditional-variance evaluation is an input oracle. This permutation
sampling procedure does not supply a conditional sampler or bound its numerical
error.

Assume AC and the positive-variance hypotheses of
[[def-dependent-input-shapley-effects]]. Then $v$ is monotone with
$v(\varnothing)=0$, $v([d])=V$, and $0\le v(S)\le V$ for every
$S\subseteq[d]$. Every $\phi_i\ge0$, and
$$\sum_{i=1}^d\phi_i=1.$$
Moreover, on the exact-oracle input for this game, the procedure
[[alg-exact-permutation-shapley-effects]] terminates after at most
$2d\,d!$ coalition-value calls and returns the Shapley effects defined above.
IID square-integrable real variables satisfy $S_n/n\to\mathbb EX_1$ almost surely.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean m and covariance Sigma. Then $$n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-m)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$ The covariance may be singular.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: Fix $i$ and $S\subseteq[d]\setminus\{i\}$. Exactly $|S|!(d-|S|-1)!$ permutations place precisely $S$ before $i$: order $S$ first, place $i$, and order the remaining coordinates last. Dividing by $d!$ gives the coefficient of $v(S\cup\{i\})-v(S)$ in the expectation of $\Delta_i$. This is exactly the Shapley weight in [F1], so $\mathbb E\Delta_i=V\phi_i$ and the estimator is unbiased.

The range and monotonicity of $v$ in [F3] give $0\le\Delta_i\le V$ for every permutation. Thus the increment vector is bounded and has finite covariance. Each increment coordinate and each pairwise product is the same measurable function of each sampled permutation; [F5] gives independence, and the common input law gives identical distributions. Apply [F4] to their coordinate and product sequences; the sample mean and covariance converge almost surely to their population values.

The bounded increment vector satisfies the finite second-moment hypothesis of [F6]. The multivariate CLT gives $\sqrt n(\bar\Delta-\mathbb E\Delta)\Rightarrow N(0,\operatorname{Cov}(\Delta))$. Scaling by the fixed positive $V$ and using step 1.1 gives the stated joint limit for $\widehat\phi$. Step 1.2 gives consistency of the covariance and standard-error estimates.

For each of the $n$ rows, the procedure traverses $d$ entries and requests two coalition values per entry. The loops are finite, so it terminates after $n$ rows and makes at most $2nd$ oracle calls. Computing the $d$ sample means and the $d\times d$ sample covariance from these rows takes $O(nd^2)$ arithmetic operations; this excludes permutation generation and oracle costs.

and let $(E,\mathcal E,\mu)=\prod_{j=1}^d(E_j,\mathcal E_j,\mu_j)$ be their
finite product with product sigma-algebra and product probability. Write
$[d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}$. For $J\subseteq[d]$, let $E_J$ and $\mu_J$ denote the
corresponding coordinate product; the empty product is a one-point probability
space. For real $f\in L^2(\mu)$, define the coordinate average
$$P_Jf(x_J)=\int_{E_{[d]\setminus J}}f(x_J,z_{[d]\setminus J})\,d\mu_{[d]\setminus J}(z_{[d]\setminus J})$$
for almost every $x_J$ for which the section is integrable, and assign zero on
the exceptional null set. Regard $P_Jf$ also as a function on the full product
that is constant in the coordinates outside $J$. The conventions are
$P_{[d]}f=f$ as an $L^2$ class and $P_\varnothing f=\int f\,d\mu$.

For the product-coordinate averages of [[def-product-coordinate-projections]],
each $P_J$ is a well-defined self-adjoint contraction on real $L^2(\mu)$,
$P_J^2=P_J$, and for all $J,K\subseteq[d]$,
$$P_JP_K=P_{J\cap K}$$
as operators on $L^2(\mu)$.

Let $f\in L^2(\mu)$ on the finite product probability space of
[[def-product-coordinate-projections]]. For $u\subseteq[d]$, its
**Hoeffding ANOVA component** indexed by $u$ is the $L^2$ class
$$f_u:=\sum_{v\subseteq u}(-1)^{|u|-|v|}P_vf.$$
In particular $f_\varnothing=P_\varnothing f=\mathbb E f$. This convention
includes all interaction orders up to $d$; $f_u$ depends only on coordinates in
$u$ once the coordinate averages are identified with their lifts to the full
product.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$

- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is

probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Since $P_uf_u=f_u$, the projection composition rule [F2] and step 2.1 give $Qf_u=QP_uf_u=P_{u\setminus\{i\}}f_u=0$. Since $P_wf_w=f_w$ and $i\notin w$, the same rule gives $Qf_w=QP_wf_w=P_wf_w=f_w$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $d\ge1$ be finite, let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$ have a finite product
probability law, and let $f(X)\in L^2$. With the components of
[[def-product-hoeffding-anova-components]],
$$f=\sum_{u\subseteq[d]}f_u\quad\text{in }L^2,$$
each $f_u$ depends only on $X_u$, every nonempty component has mean zero,
and for every $i\in u$ its coordinate average satisfies
$P_{u\setminus\{i\}}f_u=0$. Distinct components are orthogonal, and
$$\operatorname{Var}(f(X))=\sum_{\varnothing\ne u\subseteq[d]}\mathbb E[f_u(X_u)^2].$$

For the product-coordinate averages of [[def-product-coordinate-projections]],
each $P_J$ is a well-defined self-adjoint contraction on real $L^2(\mu)$,
$P_J^2=P_J$, and for all $J,K\subseteq[d]$,
$$P_JP_K=P_{J\cap K}$$
as operators on $L^2(\mu)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

Then the following four assertions are equivalent:

1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$;
2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$;
3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$
   for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]);
4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$
   converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$.

Assertion 2 is the statement
$\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$
([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Let $f\in L^2(\mu)$ on a finite product probability law and let $V_u$ denote
$\mathbb E[f_u^2]$ for the components of
[[thm-product-hoeffding-anova-decomposition]]. Write
$V=\operatorname{Var}(f)=\sum_{u\ne\varnothing}V_u$. Only when $V>0$ define
the **first-order Sobol index** and **total Sobol index** of coordinate $i$ by
$$S_i:=\frac{V_{\{i\}}}{V},\qquad S_{T_i}:=\frac{\sum_{u\ni i}V_u}{V}.$$
For $V=0$, these normalized indices are undefined. The unnormalized numerators
remain well-defined and equal zero for a constant output.

derivations.claim: For a tensor $\psi_\alpha$ and $J\subseteq[d]$, the product integral defining $P_J\psi_\alpha$ factors by [F5]. If every nonconstant coordinate of $\alpha$ lies in $J$, every integrated factor is $\phi_{j,0}=1$, so $P_J\psi_\alpha=\psi_\alpha$. If some $j\notin J$ has $\alpha_j\ne0$, its factor has mean zero, so $P_J\psi_\alpha=0$.

Let $F$ be a finite set of multi-indices and $f_F=\sum_{\alpha\in F}c_\alpha\psi_\alpha$. By [F1] and step 1.1, the coefficient of $c_\alpha\psi_\alpha$ in $(f_F)_u$ is zero when $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha)\not\subseteq u$; otherwise it is $\sum_{\operatorname{supp}(\alpha)\subseteq v\subseteq u}(-1)^{|u|-|v|}=(1-1)^{|u|-|\operatorname{supp}(\alpha)|}$. This equals one exactly when $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha)=u$ and zero otherwise. Hence $(f_F)_u=\sum_{\alpha\in F:\operatorname{supp}(\alpha)=u}c_\alpha\psi_\alpha$.

By [F4], completeness means the tensor family's closed span is all of $L^2(\mu)$. With [A1], Parseval [F3] gives $f_F\to f$ in $L^2$ as the finite-subset net increases through the tensor family. Each $Q_u:f\mapsto f_u$ is a finite signed sum of contractions $P_v$ by [F2], so $Q_uf_F\to Q_uf=f_u$ in $L^2$. Orthonormality and step 2.1 give $\|Q_uf_F\|_2^2=\sum_{\alpha\in F:\operatorname{supp}(\alpha)=u}c_\alpha^2$. These nondecreasing finite subsums converge to the nonnegative sum over all indices with support $u$; continuity of the norm then yields $V_u=\sum_{\operatorname{supp}(\alpha)=u}c_\alpha^2$.

The constant tensor is $\psi_0=1$, so the real $L^2$ pairing [F6] gives $c_0=\langle f,1\rangle=\mathbb E f$. Parseval [F3] applied to $f-c_0$ gives $\operatorname{Var}(f)=\sum_{\alpha\ne0}c_\alpha^2$. Grouping these nonnegative terms by support and substituting the component identities from step 3.1 into [F7] proves both normalized formulas when $V>0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $d\ge1$ be finite, let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$ have a finite product
probability law, and let $f(X)\in L^2$. With the components of
[[def-product-hoeffding-anova-components]],
$$f=\sum_{u\subseteq[d]}f_u\quad\text{in }L^2,$$
each $f_u$ depends only on $X_u$, every nonempty component has mean zero,
and for every $i\in u$ its coordinate average satisfies
$P_{u\setminus\{i\}}f_u=0$. Distinct components are orthogonal, and
$$\operatorname{Var}(f(X))=\sum_{\varnothing\ne u\subseteq[d]}\mathbb E[f_u(X_u)^2].$$

Let $f\in L^2(\mu)$ on a finite product probability law and let $V_u$ denote
$\mathbb E[f_u^2]$ for the components of
[[thm-product-hoeffding-anova-decomposition]]. Write
$V=\operatorname{Var}(f)=\sum_{u\ne\varnothing}V_u$. Only when $V>0$ define
the **first-order Sobol index** and **total Sobol index** of coordinate $i$ by
$$S_i:=\frac{V_{\{i\}}}{V},\qquad S_{T_i}:=\frac{\sum_{u\ni i}V_u}{V}.$$
For $V=0$, these normalized indices are undefined. The unnormalized numerators
remain well-defined and equal zero for a constant output.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $I=[a,b]$ with $L=b-a>0$,
let $g:I\to\mathbb R$ be absolutely continuous, and suppose $g'\in L^2(I)$.
Let $U$ have the uniform law $\mathbb P(U\in A)=\lambda(A\cap I)/L$. Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(g(U))\le \frac{L^2}{\pi^2}\,\mathbb E|g'(U)|^2.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $d\ge1$ be finite, let $(E_j,\mathcal E_j,\mu_j)$ be probability spaces,
and let $(E,\mathcal E,\mu)=\prod_{j=1}^d(E_j,\mathcal E_j,\mu_j)$ be their
finite product with product sigma-algebra and product probability. Write
$[d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}$. For $J\subseteq[d]$, let $E_J$ and $\mu_J$ denote the
corresponding coordinate product; the empty product is a one-point probability
space. For real $f\in L^2(\mu)$, define the coordinate average
$$P_Jf(x_J)=\int_{E_{[d]\setminus J}}f(x_J,z_{[d]\setminus J})\,d\mu_{[d]\setminus J}(z_{[d]\setminus J})$$
for almost every $x_J$ for which the section is integrable, and assign zero on
the exceptional null set. Regard $P_Jf$ also as a function on the full product
that is constant in the coordinates outside $J$. The conventions are
$P_{[d]}f=f$ as an $L^2$ class and $P_\varnothing f=\int f\,d\mu$.

For the product-coordinate averages of [[def-product-coordinate-projections]],
each $P_J$ is a well-defined self-adjoint contraction on real $L^2(\mu)$,
$P_J^2=P_J$, and for all $J,K\subseteq[d]$,
$$P_JP_K=P_{J\cap K}$$
as operators on $L^2(\mu)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

**Input:** a finite product probability law $\mu$, an evaluator $f\in L^2(\mu)$,
and a sample size $n\ge2$. Draw $n$ independent rows. In each row draw six
mutually independent vectors $X,X',U,V,W,W'$ with law $\mu$. Reuse $Y=f(X)$;
for each $i\in[d]$, evaluate the hybrids
$$X^{[i]}=(X_i,X'_{-i}),\qquad \widetilde X^{[i]}=(X_{-i},X'_i),$$
and form
$$N_i=f(X)f(X^{[i]})-f(U)f(V),\quad T_i=\tfrac12(f(X)-f(\widetilde X^{[i]}))^2,\quad D=\tfrac12(f(W)-f(W'))^2.$$
For the $n$ rows, compute their sample means $\bar N_i,\bar T_i,\bar D$ and
the unbiased sample covariance matrix $\widehat\Sigma$ of
$$Z=(N_1,\ldots,N_d,T_1,\ldots,T_d,D).$$
If $\bar D=0$, return status `zero-empirical-variance` and no normalized index.
If $\bar D>0$, return the raw ratios $\widehat S_i=\bar N_i/\bar D$ and
$\widehat S_{T_i}=\bar T_i/\bar D$. Also return the first-order plug-in MCSE
covariance matrix $\widehat J\widehat\Sigma\widehat J^{\mathsf T}/n$, where
$\widehat J$ is the derivative of the vector ratio map evaluated at
$(\bar N_1,\ldots,\bar N_d,\bar T_1,\ldots,\bar T_d,\bar D)$.
No clipping is applied to a negative finite-sample ratio.

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$ have a finite product probability law $\mu$,
$f\in L^2(\mu)$, and $\mu_f=\mathbb E[f(X)]$. Let $X'$ be an independent
copy of $X$. For $i\in[d]$, define the first-order hybrid
$X^{[i]}=(X_i,X'_{-i})$ and the total-effect hybrid
$\widetilde X^{[i]}=(X_{-i},X'_i)$. Then
$$\mathbb E[(f(X)-\mu_f)(f(X^{[i]})-\mu_f)]=V_{\{i\}},\qquad \frac12\mathbb E[(f(X)-f(\widetilde X^{[i]}))^2]=\sum_{u\ni i}V_u,$$
where $V_u=\mathbb E[f_u^2]$ are the variance components of
[[thm-product-hoeffding-anova-decomposition]]. The first covariance is an
unbiased numerator for the first-order index and the half squared difference
is an unbiased numerator for the total index; normalizing by $V$ is defined
only when $V>0$.
IID square-integrable real variables satisfy $S_n/n\to\mathbb EX_1$ almost surely.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

If $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ are IID real random variables and $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, then, with $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$ and $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|\longrightarrow0.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. On a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, let
$d\ge1$ be finite and let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$ be any jointly distributed
finite family of random elements. Let $Y=f(X)\in L^2(\mathbb P)$, and put
$V=\operatorname{Var}(Y)$. For $S\subseteq[d]$, set
$\mathcal G_S=\sigma(X_j:j\in S)$, with $\mathcal G_\varnothing=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$, and
$$v(S)=\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal G_S]).$$
If $V>0$, let $\mathfrak S_d$ be the set of all $d!$ permutations of $[d]$,
and let $P_i^\pi$ contain the indices occurring before $i$ in $\pi$. The
**Shapley effect** of coordinate $i$ under this convention is
$$\phi_i=\frac{1}{d!\,V}\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak S_d}\bigl(v(P_i^\pi\cup\{i\})-v(P_i^\pi)\bigr).$$
If $V=0$, the normalized effects are undefined. This definition is for
dependent inputs as well as independent ones; the independent Sobol ANOVA
components are not used to define $v$.

[[def-dependent-input-shapley-effects]]. Then $v$ is monotone with
$v(\varnothing)=0$, $v([d])=V$, and $0\le v(S)\le V$ for every
$S\subseteq[d]$. Every $\phi_i\ge0$, and
$$\sum_{i=1}^d\phi_i=1.$$
Moreover, on the exact-oracle input for this game, the procedure
[[alg-exact-permutation-shapley-effects]] terminates after at most
$2d\,d!$ coalition-value calls and returns the Shapley effects defined above.

variance game of [[def-dependent-input-shapley-effects]].

2. For each of the $d!$ permutations $\pi$, traverse its entries in order. Start
   with $S=\varnothing$. At entry $i$, add $v(S\cup\{i\})-v(S)$ to $A_i$ and

not approximate conditional expectations or their numerical errors.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, independent real random variables
$Y_1,\ldots,Y_d$ with marginal Borel probability laws $\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_d$,
and a degree cutoff vector $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$. Their joint
law is $\rho=\rho_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_d$ on $\mathbb R^d$, as in
[[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]]. For a Borel
probability law $\rho_j$ on $\mathbb R$, define
$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho_j):=\{x\in\mathbb R:\rho_j(U)>0\text{ for every open }U\ni x\}.$$
The complement is a union of zero-measure members of the countable rational
interval basis, so countable additivity gives
$\rho_j(\operatorname{supp}(\rho_j))=1$. Set
$\Gamma=\prod_{j=1}^d\operatorname{supp}(\rho_j)$ and give it the trace Borel
sigma-algebra from $\mathbb R^d$. The product rectangle formula gives
$\rho(\Gamma)=1$. Whenever the measure space is written as
$(\Gamma,\mathcal B(\Gamma),\rho)$, $\rho$ denotes the restriction of the
product law on $\mathbb R^d$ to $\mathcal B(\Gamma)$; it is therefore a
probability measure. The product rectangle formula also identifies this
restriction with the finite product of the marginal laws restricted to their
supports. The cutoff vector $p$ is **admissible** when, for every
$j=1,\ldots,d$,
$$\int |y|^{2p_j}\,d\rho_j(y)<\infty$$
and the monomial Gram matrix
$$G_j=(\int y^{r+s}\,d\rho_j(y))_{0\le r,s\le p_j}$$
is positive definite, meaning $c^T G_jc>0$ for each nonzero
$c\in\mathbb R^{p_j+1}$. Throughout the pair, assume the selected cutoff
vector is admissible. The admissible degree box is
$\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\alpha_j\le p_j\text{ for every }j\}$.
Admissibility gives a finite inner product on each stated polynomial space.
It is only a finite-degree condition; it does not assert that polynomials are
dense in any $L^2(\rho_j)$.

Let $\rho_j$ be one factor law with admissible degree $p_j$ as in
[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]]. The monomial classes
$1,y,\ldots,y^{p_j}$ are linearly independent in $L^2(\rho_j)$. Applying the
finite Gram–Schmidt recursion to this ordered list gives real orthonormal
polynomials $\phi_{j,0},\ldots,\phi_{j,p_j}$, where $\phi_{j,k}$ has degree
$k$, positive leading coefficient, and $\phi_{j,0}=1$.

Let $\phi_{j,k}$ be the Gram–Schmidt polynomials from
[[lem-positive-moment-gram-produces-univariate-chaos-polynomials]], and let
$\Lambda$ be a finite subset of the admissible degree box in
[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]]. For $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)\in\Lambda$,
define
$$\psi_\alpha(y_1,\ldots,y_d)=\prod_{j=1}^d\phi_{j,\alpha_j}(y_j).$$
Here $L^2(\rho)$ uses the full-mass restriction to $\Gamma$ specified in
[[def-finite-product-chaos-input]], which the product rectangle formula
identifies with the product of the restricted marginal laws.
The **finite polynomial-chaos space** is
$\mathcal P_\Lambda=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_\alpha:\alpha\in\Lambda\}$
inside $L^2(\rho)$. Whenever $0\in\Lambda$ (in particular, for the stated
total-degree and hyperbolic-cross sets), the family contains the constant mode
$\psi_0=1$. No density of $\mathcal P_\Lambda$ in $L^2(\rho)$ is part of this
definition.

Let $d\ge1$ be finite, let $(E_j,\mathcal E_j,\mu_j)$ be probability spaces,
and let $(E,\mathcal E,\mu)=\prod_{j=1}^d(E_j,\mathcal E_j,\mu_j)$ be their
finite product with product sigma-algebra and product probability. Write
$[d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}$. For $J\subseteq[d]$, let $E_J$ and $\mu_J$ denote the
corresponding coordinate product; the empty product is a one-point probability
space. For real $f\in L^2(\mu)$, define the coordinate average
$$P_Jf(x_J)=\int_{E_{[d]\setminus J}}f(x_J,z_{[d]\setminus J})\,d\mu_{[d]\setminus J}(z_{[d]\setminus J})$$
for almost every $x_J$ for which the section is integrable, and assign zero on
the exceptional null set. Regard $P_Jf$ also as a function on the full product
that is constant in the coordinates outside $J$. The conventions are
$P_{[d]}f=f$ as an $L^2$ class and $P_\varnothing f=\int f\,d\mu$.

Let $d\ge1$ be finite, let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$ have a finite product
probability law, and let $f(X)\in L^2$. With the components of
[[def-product-hoeffding-anova-components]],
$$f=\sum_{u\subseteq[d]}f_u\quad\text{in }L^2,$$
each $f_u$ depends only on $X_u$, every nonempty component has mean zero,
and for every $i\in u$ its coordinate average satisfies
$P_{u\setminus\{i\}}f_u=0$. Distinct components are orthogonal, and
$$\operatorname{Var}(f(X))=\sum_{\varnothing\ne u\subseteq[d]}\mathbb E[f_u(X_u)^2].$$

Let $f\in L^2(\mu)$ on a finite product probability law and let $V_u$ denote
$\mathbb E[f_u^2]$ for the components of
[[thm-product-hoeffding-anova-decomposition]]. Write
$V=\operatorname{Var}(f)=\sum_{u\ne\varnothing}V_u$. Only when $V>0$ define
the **first-order Sobol index** and **total Sobol index** of coordinate $i$ by
$$S_i:=\frac{V_{\{i\}}}{V},\qquad S_{T_i}:=\frac{\sum_{u\ni i}V_u}{V}.$$
For $V=0$, these normalized indices are undefined. The unnormalized numerators
remain well-defined and equal zero for a constant output.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$ have a finite product probability law $\mu$,
$f\in L^2(\mu)$, and $\mu_f=\mathbb E[f(X)]$. Let $X'$ be an independent
copy of $X$. For $i\in[d]$, define the first-order hybrid
$X^{[i]}=(X_i,X'_{-i})$ and the total-effect hybrid
$\widetilde X^{[i]}=(X_{-i},X'_i)$. Then
$$\mathbb E[(f(X)-\mu_f)(f(X^{[i]})-\mu_f)]=V_{\{i\}},\qquad \frac12\mathbb E[(f(X)-f(\widetilde X^{[i]}))^2]=\sum_{u\ni i}V_u,$$
where $V_u=\mathbb E[f_u^2]$ are the variance components of
[[thm-product-hoeffding-anova-decomposition]]. The first covariance is an
unbiased numerator for the first-order index and the half squared difference
is an unbiased numerator for the total index; normalizing by $V$ is defined
only when $V>0$.

Let $f\in L^2(\mu)$ on a finite product probability law and let $V_u$ denote
$\mathbb E[f_u^2]$ for the components of
[[thm-product-hoeffding-anova-decomposition]]. Write
$V=\operatorname{Var}(f)=\sum_{u\ne\varnothing}V_u$. Only when $V>0$ define
the **first-order Sobol index** and **total Sobol index** of coordinate $i$ by
$$S_i:=\frac{V_{\{i\}}}{V},\qquad S_{T_i}:=\frac{\sum_{u\ni i}V_u}{V}.$$
For $V=0$, these normalized indices are undefined. The unnormalized numerators
remain well-defined and equal zero for a constant output.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

derivations.claim: Put $\mathcal G=\sigma(X)$. For each $A\in\mathcal G$, independence [F1]–[F2] factors $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A\epsilon]=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb E\epsilon=0$. Thus the $\mathcal G$-measurable integrable variable $f(X)$ satisfies $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A Y]=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A f(X)]$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$, so [F7] identifies $\mathbb E[Y\mid X]=f(X)$. Also [F8] makes the cross moment integrable, and the same independence factorization gives $\operatorname{Cov}(f(X),\epsilon)=0$. Expanding variance by [F3] and using linearity [F9] yields $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=V_f+\tau^2$, where $V_f=\operatorname{Var}(f(X))$.

In a first-order pick-freeze pair with fresh independent noise at both evaluations, the covariance of the two outputs is $\operatorname{Cov}(f(X),f(X^{[i]}))$: all cross covariances with noise vanish by the product factorization, and the two noise copies have zero covariance. The required products are integrable by [F8]. By [F5], this numerator is $V_{\{i\}}(f)$. Dividing by $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$ yields $V_{\{i\}}(f)/(V_f+\tau^2)$, while the conditional-mean index is $V_{\{i\}}(f)/V_f$ only if $V_f>0$ and is undefined if $V_f=0$.

In a total-effect pair, expand $Y-\widetilde Y=(f(X)-f(\widetilde X^{[i]}))+ (\epsilon-\epsilon')$. The cross term has zero expectation because the noises are centered and independent of inputs; [F8] ensures its integrability. Linearity [F9] and independence give $\frac12\mathbb E[(\epsilon-\epsilon')^2]=\tau^2$. Thus half the expected squared difference is the input total-effect numerator from [F5] plus $\tau^2$. Therefore raw noisy total-effect estimation includes intrinsic noise unless the target is the conditional mean or the noise term is separately accounted for.
